_comment: Shown on the dashboard after an update: the versions newer than the one this browser last saw, newest first. Add an entry with each release, in the version bump. A few short lines each; the full notes are on the release page.

items: There is a new Tools tab, beside Activity. Ping now runs live, with a line of the last minute and the average, loss and jitter. Trace route and Path ping show each hop as a row with its time and where the delay starts. A DNS lookup asks your own DNS server and, for a name you type, Cloudflare and Google too. New HTTP check and Port check. And a Why is it slow? button checks your router, your DNS server, the internet and a web name and says where it breaks.
A device's menu now opens the Tools tab on that device. Typing an address that isn't one of your devices still needs the Tools to any address setting, which is off until you switch it on.
Select moved next to the filters on the Devices tab, Pause alerts is a button in the header that says when alerts are held, and the Tools menu is now called More.

Alerts can now go to Slack, Telegram or an email address. Paste a Slack or Telegram webhook URL and BAMF recognises it, and under Settings, Alerts, More destinations there is a new Email option: a mail server, your login if it asks, and who to send to. Email takes the same choice of what it gets, waits out quiet hours and is retried when the mail server is down. Its password is kept on this machine and never shown again.

BAMF can tell you when your public IP address changes, which is usually the modem restarting and breaks anything that reaches your network by its address. It is off until you switch it on under Settings, Internet, because it asks Cloudflare every 15 minutes.
BAMF can also tell you when it is signed into from an address that never has been. Off until you switch it on under Settings, Security, Sign-in.
The network score now counts a DNS server that gives wrong answers and an internet connection with quality problems.

BAMF now watches what devices do, not just whether they are there. A new Where devices talk card on Activity shows which outside networks each device talks to; after a week, a camera, plug or thermostat that starts talking somewhere new is an alert. A device scanning the network, or moving far more in a day than usual, is an alert too, and every new device gets a report after its first week. Each has a switch under Settings, Security, What devices do.

A DNS watch, off until you switch it on under Settings, Security: once an hour it checks that your resolver gives the right answers for names that never change, says no such name when it should, and hasn't been joined by a server you never saw before.

The internet watch now measures quality as well as up or down: lost pings, jitter and how long a DNS lookup takes, on the Internet card, with alerts when any of them goes wrong for a quarter of an hour. Switch under Settings, Internet.
A watched device that is slow to answer for five pings running is an alert, and so is its coming right. The limit is yours to set under Settings, Scanning.

A network score, 0 to 100, with the reasons it isn't 100, on Activity and at the top of scheduled reports. And a daily all-quiet note, off by default under Settings, Alerts: one message a day saying nothing happened, or what did.

Alerts are more dependable and quieter. An alert a destination refuses is tried again after 1, 5, 15 and 30 minutes instead of being lost. A device that keeps dropping gets one alert saying so, and when a switch goes down you get one alert, such as Rack switch went offline and 14 devices behind it, instead of one for each device. Each has its own switch in Settings, under Alerts.

Tools can now ping and trace the route to any address you type, including ones on the internet. Path ping traces the route and then pings every router on the way, to show where the trouble starts. It is off until you switch it on in Settings, under System, and it needs the main password.
A device's menu has a new Path ping next to Trace route.

BAMF now watches its own disk. A new Disk and database card on the Activity tab shows how big the database and backups are and how much room is left, and BAMF raises an alert when the drive is running low, which used to show up only as failed backups. The percentage, or switching it off, is in Settings under System.
Select devices has an Undo. After a bulk change such as forgetting twelve devices, an Undo button puts every one of them back exactly as it was, including their tags, watch and snooze.

A new Views menu saves the device list the way you have set it up, such as a network, a status, a device type, a tag and a search, under a name like Kids' devices offline. Pick one later and the list is set to match in one click.

A device's menu now has Ping, Trace route and DNS lookup under Look closer. They run from the machine BAMF is on and only ever at that device's own address. You can switch them off in Settings, under System.
The Activity tab shows a small number of what has appeared since you last looked there. It is a setting in this browser, under Appearance.

Fixes a bug in 2.5.0 and 2.6.0 where thirteen dialogs never appeared: Snooze alerts, Pause alerts, notes, tags, device type, the ports and switch dialogs and more. Clicking them looked like it did nothing. They all open again.
The Problems card now sits after the hygiene card on the Activity tab, so the Internet card is no longer stretched beside the tall Network services card.

A new Problems card on the Activity tab lists what has gone wrong inside BAMF since it started: an alert a webhook refused, a router that would not take its password, a scan that failed. Until now that only went to a log file on the server.

BAMF now says so when it starts again after stopping unexpectedly, such as after a power cut or a crash, with how long it was down. Stopping the service or updating stays quiet. You can switch this off in Settings, under Alerts.

Tools has two new entries. Pause alerts holds every alert for a while, for when you are about to reboot a switch, and sends what came up as one summary afterwards. Select devices puts tick boxes on the list so you can mark, watch, ignore, tag, snooze or forget several devices at once.

A new Heartbeat in Settings visits an address you give it, such as a Healthchecks.io ping, every few minutes, so a monitoring service can tell you when BAMF itself goes quiet. It is off until you set it up.
Tidy up old devices can forget devices nobody has touched that have been gone a long time. It is off until you switch it on, and nothing is deleted: they go to the Forgotten tab.
Pause alerts and Select devices each have a switch in Settings if you would rather not have them.

A new Report for my provider link on the Internet card opens one printable page of the last 30 days: outages on the line, slow spells and speed tests. Outages that took your own router down too are listed apart, so you only send your provider what is theirs.
If you watch other BAMF servers, a Sites card on the Activity tab puts them side by side with this one. BAMF now also raises an alert when one of them stops answering, and another when it is back.
Settings has Export settings and Import settings: set up a second BAMF the way the first one is. Passwords, webhook addresses, the site's networks and the devices stay behind.

Devices have 26 more types, each with its own Map icon: streamer, soundbar, thermostat, doorbell, smart lock, robot vacuum, fridge, 3D printer, modem, mesh node, Raspberry Pi and more. BAMF now reads a device's name and vendor to pick them, so a Roku shows as a streamer rather than a TV.
The Network services card has a Look it up button: it asks Cloudflare which public address your home shows to the internet and records it, with no speed test needed.

The Christmas theme is rebuilt as a winter night: northern lights, a moon, mountains, pines, falling snow and a house whose chimney smokes and sometimes has Santa in it. The page gets a candy-cane header, icicles, snow on the cards and a candy-cane scrollbar.

The Halloween theme is rebuilt as a haunted night: a big moon with clouds crossing it, a haunted house on a hill with flickering windows, a graveyard and dead trees, lanterns that light the corners, and lightning now and then.
Crows fly over, a witch crosses the moon, ghosts drift up and a skeleton hand rises from the ground. The headings drip in a spooky font, and slime drips from the header.
A new device you haven't marked known is still a werewolf at the graveyard gate, now under a blood moon that reddens the whole sky.
Holiday Spirit switches it on for October. With reduced motion the scene holds still.

A new Network services card on the Activity tab lists what BAMF has seen providing a service on your network: your public address, each network's gateway, DHCP and DNS servers, UPnP and mDNS, and which devices offer what (web pages, SSH, file sharing, printing, AirPlay and more). It replaces Network watch, with the same Trust and Forget buttons.
Your public address is learned from the speed test and the daily GreyNoise check, with where it came from and what it was before it changed. Nothing new is sent to learn it.

Under it, BAMF's own connections: what it reads from, sends to and calls out to, and whether each is working, like a router import, MQTT, backups or the speed test. What isn't set up is a line of links to its Settings.

The default port scan grows from 18 to 34 ports, adding camera streams, AirPlay, Home Assistant, databases and more. A device already listening on one of them isn't alerted about it the first time it's scanned for it.

BAMF 2.0 learns what's normal for each device and says when something isn't: a device that's almost always on, off far longer than it ever is; a device on at an hour it never is; or one answering much slower than usual.

What it notices is on the Activity tab's new Unusual card, and is an alert of a new kind, Unusual activity: tick it under Sends to have these sent to you. That's normal beside one stops it being flagged for that again for 30 days.
Each device needs two weeks of history first, so for a newly added one it's quiet to begin with. Settings, under Alerts, switches it off.
The nightly backups' second folder, a NAS share say, can now be set in Settings, under System. BAMF checks it can write there when you save.

BAMF now backs itself up every night, at 3 am unless you pick another hour in Settings, under System. It keeps the newest 7, with appsettings.json alongside, and a night the machine was off it catches up.
Backups on this machine, in the same card, lists every backup on the server, each with a Restore button. What a restore replaces is kept, so it can be undone.
Set Bamf:Backup:CopyTo in appsettings.json to copy each night's backup to a second folder, a NAS share say.
On Linux, the installer switches off the old backup timer, since BAMF now does it itself.
Home Assistant gets more over MQTT: devices online, unknown devices (with their names), and whether the internet is up, ready for automations like a phone alert when an unknown device joins.
A log of settings changes on the Activity tab: what changed, when, with which password and from where. Only each setting's name is kept, never its value.
An alert 14 and 3 days before BAMF's own HTTPS certificate runs out, from the morning certificate watch.
Number boxes in Settings now fit five digits, like 3600 seconds for the internet check.

MQTT, other BAMF servers and the inbound webhooks' token are in Settings, under System, and apply without a restart. Saved passwords are never shown again, and only go back to the server they were saved for.

HTTPS in one click: Settings, Security, HTTPS makes a certificate for this machine, and after a restart BAMF also serves the dashboard at https://<server>:8843. Browsers warn once, since nothing vouches for it.
On a phone's home screen BAMF now has its own icon and opens in a window of its own, with the status bar in your theme's colour.
Under the hood, the dashboard and the server are split into files by what they do. Nothing about how they work has changed.

Passwords in Settings, under Security: set, change or remove the main and view-only passwords here, kept hashed. With one set, a browser signs in on a page of its own and stays signed in for 30 days; scripts and Home Assistant send it as before.
Five wrong passwords from one address lock it out for 15 minutes, with a security alert. A forgotten password is reset from the machine BAMF runs on; the README says how.
Add and remove the networks BAMF watches in Settings, under Scanning, with one click for each network this machine is on.
A new install asks two things the first time it opens: which networks to watch, and a password.
Updated parts: a newer SQLite, which keeps BAMF's database, and a newer packet-capture library for the active ARP scan and the traffic monitor.
BAMF now runs on .NET 10. .NET 8, which it ran on before, stops getting security updates on November 10.
Building from source, as the Windows updater and Linux installer do, now needs the .NET 10 SDK. The Linux installer fetches it; the Windows updater tells you if it's missing and changes nothing.
In RGB, every light on the rig now turns red for an intruder, not just the frame: the card borders, the rainbow numbers, the logo and the rest.
If you've changed BAMF's port, the Windows desktop shortcut now opens it, and the updaters show it when they finish.
The Terminal theme's description in the theme list now says what it is: Battlezone, with a tank for each unknown device.

Every animated and holiday theme now has an intruder: a werewolf at Halloween, a yeti in Winter, a fox after the hens in Spring, a stranger struck by lightning in the Thunderstorm, a seagull after the hot dogs, a burglar on the naughty list, and more.
Waterworks locks out a leak, Terminal traces and quarantines, Laser Show holds a rogue droid in every beam, and RGB finds a strange stick plugged into the rig.
When two intruders are held and one is marked known, the other no longer lands on top of it as it goes.

Eleven more themes treat a new device you haven't marked known as an intruder, sixteen in all: a police chase in City Lights, lockdown in the Data Centre, an Agent in Matrix, a bear in Woodlands, TILT in the Claw Machine, and more.
Each raises the alarm, then holds the intruder, tagged, until you mark it known. Show me an intruder, in Settings, Appearance, plays the one in your theme.
The README now opens with a short video.
Themes update reliably on Windows: 1.52.0 could leave some on their old versions, or take one out of the menu. This puts them right.
If one theme can't be updated, the rest still are.
In Harbour, Ant Farm, Model Railway, Goat and Aquarium, a new device you haven't marked known is an intruder: the scene raises the alarm, then holds it, tagged, until you mark it known.
A ship with no lights, a beetle, a rogue engine, a wolf, a shark. Marking the device known stands the scene down.
Show me an intruder, in Settings, Appearance, plays the scene on one of your devices.
Themes are now folders you can add and remove: Settings, Appearance, Themes shows every one with a picture. Dark, Light and High Contrast are built in.
A theme someone shares is a .zip: add it there, or drop it into the themes folder and reload.
The dashboard is about half the size, since a theme loads only when it's picked.
The watchman's hat now sits properly on his head.
On the watchtower, a new device's alert now stays until you mark it known or dismiss it, with buttons under the callout.
While an alert is up, moving the mouse brings up the pointer for those buttons instead of waking the page.
Show me an alert, in Settings, Appearance, previews one on one of your devices.
A new screen saver, the watchtower: a watchman keeps watch over your network from a tower by moonlight, his searchlight sweeping the yard where every device stands.
A new device sets off a jailbreak: beacons, the night gone red, and the light locked onto it with its details.
Pick it under Settings, Appearance, Screen saver, with or without the siren.
A screen saver: after a while idle, the dashboard fades and leaves the theme's scenery, with a small card of how many devices are online. Turn it on in Settings, Appearance.
The New tab now drops a device once you mark it known, so it's the list of devices you haven't dealt with yet.
How many days a device counts as new is a setting, under Settings, Your network.
Two new themes: Harbour, where every device is a container on the quay, and Ant Farm, where every device has a chamber in the nest.
This note: after an update, BAMF says what changed. The version in the header shows it any time.
On a phone, the Activity tab no longer slides sideways.
Settings is in seven sections, picked from a list down the side, with a box to find any setting.
Each section has its own address, such as /#settings/internet.
Appearance has a Theme row, beside Holiday Spirit and Night mode.
A device's ⋯ menu is grouped: About this device, Wiring, Look closer and Status.
Scan ▾ in the header: sweep every network or one right now, scan ports, or run the health check.
Test beside your saved webhook in Settings, in place of Tools → Test webhook.
The hygiene card's Check now is the Scan menu's Health check.
A scheduled speed test that fails, say just after the machine wakes, is tried twice more within the hour.
Speed test: download, upload and ping against Cloudflare, from Run now on the Internet card or on a schedule.
A month of tests is charted, and a scheduled test well under your usual is an Internet alert.
Spring and Summer have ground of their own along the bottom, clear of the table, and are a shade softer.
Data Centre has a hologram of your network, a shuttle with a scan laser, and readouts on the patch panel.
